title: Philip Rivers finalizing agreement to return to NC State as Wolfpack’s new head coach in remarkable move
excerpt:
"There are no dominant teams in college football. There's no juggernaut out there. Like this time a year ago, you really could tell Indiana was legitimate, that they were a powerhouse."

After N.C. St...
body_text:
"There are no dominant teams in college football. There's no juggernaut out there. Like this time a year ago, you really could tell Indiana was legitimate, that they were a powerhouse."

After N.C. State officials made the trek to Fairhope, Alabama earlier this week to formally meet with Philip Rivers, the former Wolfpack and NFL quarterback appears to be set to take the head coaching position at his alma mater.

The two sides are finalizing an agreement that is expected to be hammered out over the next 24 hours, sources told OutKick. The board of trustees at N.C. State have a meeting this coming week to approve the contract.

Conversations about Rivers taking the job in Raleigh had picked up after the school announced that Dave Doeren had been fired nearly two weeks ago.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Following a series of informal discussions with major donors about what it would take to make N.C. State competitive in the current era of college athletics, several Wolfpack boosters put a plan in motion to provide Rivers with the resources needed to hit the ground running.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

By the end of the week, all that was needed was pen to paper for the NC State alum.

But first, Rivers was going to finish his job as head coach of St. Michael Catholic in the Alabama high school football playoffs. His season came to an end on Friday night in Fairhope, as they lost in the opening round.

Phillip Rivers of the North Carolina State Wolfpack throws a pass against the Maryland Terrapins at Byrd Stadium in College Park, Md., on Nov. 9, 2002. (Getty Images)

According to multiple sources, Rivers had already begun putting together a coaching and front office staff for when he formally accepted the job offer and signed a contract.

On Friday night, Rivers was coaching St. Michael Catholic in their Alabama high school playoff game, where his son Gunner also plays. In addition to the intrigue of coaching for the first time in college, Gunner is also committed to NC State and will enroll in January to start his own collegiate career.

One of the biggest points of emphasis for Rivers taking the job in Raleigh was that he would be given enough money to work with for a veteran coaching staff, given that this will be his first college job.

Sources tell OutKick that one of his contract asks was that he be given a big enough pool of money to attract assistant coaches with college experience that would be open to making a move to Raleigh.

Former NC State quarterback Philip Rivers attends the game between the North Carolina Tar Heels and the NC State Wolfpack at Carter-Finley Stadium in Raleigh, N.C., on Nov. 29, 2025. (Getty Images)

Also, having the NIL resources outside of the revenue-sharing that schools participate in was a key part of negotiations for NC State athletic director Boo Corrigan landing the former NFL quarterback.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL’S JERRY JONES? TEXAS TECH BOOSTER CODY CAMPBELL DEMANDS RETURN ON INVESTMENT

From a fan perspective, it's obvious that the Wolfpack would be making a hire that would excite the base, and more importantly help sell tickets and also lead to an influx of donations needed to help fund rosters in the future.

This is seen as a win-win for both sides, given that this would obviously be an interesting splash around college football, especially in recruiting players who are familiar with the new head coach.

But there is also the obvious fact that players are going to go where the money leads them, though that's clearly not the case for every player.

Still, putting together a formidable roster that can compete in the ACC and subsequently for a spot in the upcoming expanded College Football Playoff is key to making sure this hire doesn’t turn into a dud over the next few years.

NICK SABAN SPEAKS TRUTH ON CFP EXPANSION: ‘THERE’S NOT 24 TEAMS’ THAT CAN WIN A NATIONAL TITLE, BUT MONEY WINS

We have seen countless coordinators in the college ranks receive their first shot at a head coaching job and watch it turn into chaos; just look at what is taking place with Tosh Lupoi at Cal this season, where general manager Ron Rivera is already sounding the alarms.

But, for a high school coach to be given an opportunity to start their collegiate career at the top, and especially at a school like NC State, goes to show you how much Wolfpack officials think about Rivers.

Philip Rivers No. 17 of the Indianapolis Colts walks off the field at halftime against the San Francisco 49ers at Lucas Oil Stadium on Dec. 22, 2025, in Indianapolis, Ind. (Getty Images)

Now, the donors who have promised Rivers with the funds needed to compete will be tasked with making sure he can attack the transfer portal to add players to this NC State roster so that he can hit the ground running for the 2027 season.

This will be an interesting situation to watch unfold over the next few months, with NC State fans expecting this team to once again start competing for ACC titles on a yearly basis.

Welcome to college football, Philip Rivers.

Trey Wallace is the Sr. College Sports Reporter for OutKick.

title: Infantino’s Japanese challenger claims he could unseat FIFA president
excerpt:
The latest challenger to FIFA President Gianni Infantino’s re-election bid, Kozo Tashima, believes he has a 20 to 30 percent chance of winning the coveted seat in global football.

Tashima, the honora...
body_text:
The latest challenger to FIFA President Gianni Infantino’s re-election bid, Kozo Tashima, believes he has a 20 to 30 percent chance of winning the coveted seat in global football.

Tashima, the honorary president of the Japan Football Association (JFA), said governance is FIFA’s biggest problem as he outlined his platform for next year’s presidential election on Sunday.

“I’ve received many messages saying, ‘Thank you for speaking out’…,” Tashima told Japanese daily Sports Nippon.

Tashima announced on Thursday that he intended to run in the March election, becoming the first Japanese candidate to seek world football’s top job.

The 68-year-old former Japan international has served on the FIFA Council since 2015 and became JFA president the following year before being succeeded by Tsuneyasu Miyamoto in 2024.

“I’ve been contacted by presidents and international department officials from eight countries, including some outside Asia,” he said.

“While I haven’t received any formal endorsements yet, I’m getting a positive response. Since time is short and I don’t want to be held up by incomplete paperwork, I want to secure support from at least six associations.”

Tashima requires nominations from five national associations, a prerequisite for standing in the election.

Candidates have until November 18 to submit nominations for the election, in which Infantino is seeking a fourth term as head of world football’s governing body.

Infantino came under scrutiny in July after an unsuccessful attempt to bring private investors into a new FIFA commercial entity holding rights linked to competitions including the World Cup.

Despite the criticism, Infantino’s candidacy received a significant boost in October when the head of Asian football publicly endorsed him, while support from several FIFA confederations has left him well placed among the organisation’s 211 member associations.

“I’ll keep what’s good and change what’s bad…,” Tashima added. “The biggest problem, however, remains governance…

“Selflessness is my motto… At this stage, I think my chances of winning are about 20 to 30 percent, but as the campaign progresses, I want to raise my confidence to 40 or 50 percent. I truly want to change FIFA.”

Former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega was the first candidate to publicly declare his intention to challenge fellow Swiss citizen Infantino last month.

title: Climate always comes second: are green issues slipping down Burnham’s agenda?
excerpt:
Prime minister says he’s committed to meeting climate targets, but some believe his actions suggest otherwise

Labour expected to cut EV targets for car industry despite MPs’ climate concerns

Andy Bu...
body_text:
Prime minister says he’s committed to meeting climate targets, but some believe his actions suggest otherwise

Labour expected to cut EV targets for car industry despite MPs’ climate concerns

Andy Burnham insists he is committed to the green transition, but his MPs worry that in decision after decision, he is showing that other priorities come first.

“Our changing climate is a major concern for many Britons, not least because we have just emerged from our hottest summer on record,” the prime minister wrote in the Guardian in September.

Since then, however, he has overseen a series of announcements that have dismayed green-focused Labour MPs.

First his energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, approved the Jackdaw gasfield. Then his chancellor, John Healey, announced a series of cuts to green schemes such as heat pump subsidies.

Now MPs are carefully watching two key decisions to be made in the coming weeks: whether he pushes Fahnbulleh to approve the larger Rosebank oilfield, and whether his ministers cut electric vehicle targets.

“I know the prime minister is committed to the green transition and meeting our climate targets, and he understands the seriousness of the climate crisis,” said Catherine Fookes, a Labour backbencher.

But she added: “The government has some incredibly difficult decisions to make in the coming months … I believe the ZEV [zero emissions vehicle] mandate should stay, and Rosebank should be rejected.”

Her colleague Andrew Lewin said: “We have a strong record on renewables, and lots of good work being led by DESNZ [the energy department]. Approving Rosebank would risk undermining our record. It is not worth it.”

Ami McCarthy, the head of politics at Greenpeace, said: “This government’s heart seems to be in the right place on climate, but there’s still a real danger of them sleepwalking into reversing the progress made so far.”

Those close to the prime minister insist he understands the importance of tackling the climate crisis and believes it can help to bring down living costs in the future.

But, at the same time, he is trying to give voters financial “breathing space” this winter while also bolstering national security.

Some Labour MPs criticised Burnham in the summer for responding to wildfires by urging people not to use barbecues rather than talking about the climate emergency. But they have been more concerned by decisions he has taken since.

The decisions to approve Jackdaw and cut some of the energy department’s green schemes were based on national security concerns.

By providing a domestic source of gas, Jackdaw will reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels, with European dependence on Russian gas having proved a big problem at the outbreak of the war in Ukraine.

And by cutting more than £3bn from the energy department, Healey has been able to raise defence spending – something the former defence secretary has made one of his top priorities.

The cuts will come principally from the £15bn warm homes plan, which promised to roll out electrified energy via heat pumps, rooftop solar panels and batteries, and to cut energy waste via home insulation. Funding for hydrogen and carbon capture technologies has been cut by £700m.

The cuts to the boiler upgrade scheme in particular were met with dismay among environmental experts. Britain lags behind many European countries when it comes to electrifying its heating system.

Experts say the UK is now unlikely to meet its heat pump targets and may even miss its emissions reductions target in the next carbon budget.

Andrew Sissons, a director at the National Endowment for Science, Technology and the Arts, a research charity, said: “The chancellor made a backward step here. If you speak to any climate change expert they will say the biggest problem to tackle is home heating.

“We are way behind where we need to be. The most effective action to remove carbon emissions from homes is to replace gas boilers with heat pumps.

“The boiler upgrade scheme is the key mechanism for removing emissions from home heating, and cutting it sends a damaging signal to the heat pump industry.”

James Dyson, a senior researcher at the thinktank E3G, said: “Reliance on gas means the UK will remain vulnerable to economic shocks and military threats.”

Green campaigners were also disappointed by the budget decisions to allow hyperscale datacentres to build on-site fossil fuel power generation and not to increase the windfall tax on energy companies.

BP profits hit $8.5bn (£6.4bn) in the three months to September – an 18-year high – while Shell doubled its profits to $10.8bn.

Defenders of the prime minister and the chancellor deny the government has slowed its efforts to tackle the climate crisis.

They say the cuts to green schemes were originally agreed by Keir Starmer’s government, and that this government’s decision to cut VAT from electricity bills would incentivise consumers to move away from gas.

Ministers are also working on plans to remove more levies from electricity bills and to fund environmental schemes through taxation instead, something green campaigners are likely to welcome.

Danny Gross, a climate campaigner at Friends of the Earth, said: “While the chancellor stopped new levies being piled on to energy bills, he failed to remove the remaining ones that keep electricity so expensive. These should be moved to general taxation to share costs more fairly.”

For nervous Labour MPs, the decisions over Rosebank and the ZEV mandate are key.

While Fahnbulleh’s allies say she wants to block the oilfield, those close to Healey say he wants it to go ahead.

Burnham is reported to have sided with the chancellor, but No 10 officials insist the PM is happy for Fahnbulleh to make her own decision. The final outcome is due before the end of the year.

More immediately, ministers will meet this week to finalise the 2030 EV target, which the Guardian understands will be cut by about a quarter.

Again, those close to the PM say the decision reflects business reality, and has not been his to make after he recused himself because of his wife’s role at an EV charging company.

But for some in his party, it is another sign that when key judgment calls are being made, the climate is coming second every time.

One MP said: “I think Andy cares about the climate, but if every decision he makes ends up damaging it, his intentions don’t really matter.”

title: Trump set to lurch further right, claiming US took ‘giant step back’ in elections
excerpt:
Trump poised to double down on immigration crackdown and refuse concessions to new Democratic majority in Congress

Donald Trump set the stage for his administration to lurch further to the right this...
body_text:
Trump poised to double down on immigration crackdown and refuse concessions to new Democratic majority in Congress

Donald Trump set the stage for his administration to lurch further to the right this weekend, claiming the US had taken a “giant step back” by widely rejecting his party.

The US president’s hardline aide, Stephen Miller, will begin as White House chief of staff on Monday. He will also meet with Dana White, CEO and president of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, after offering him the job of press secretary.

“America took a giant step back in History with the results of the last Election,” Trump claimed in a post on his Truth Social platform on Sunday morning, citing the sharp sell-off in global markets, fueled a rout of US tech stocks. “But have no fear, we will be back, BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE!”

Despite Republicans losing control of both chambers of US Congress in Tuesday’s decisive US midterm elections, and voters across the country expressing frustration with key pillars of Trump’s controversial agenda, from the Iran war to sweeping tariffs, the administration appears set to press ahead.

Miller’s promotion has stoked expectations that Trump is poised to double down on an aggressive immigration crackdown, stoke cultural war battles, and refuse concessions to the new Democratic majority in Congress. The move “signals the administration is going to ⁠have a fighting-from-a-bunker approach the last two years”, Dan Eberhart, a Trump donor and energy executive, told Reuters.

Trump abruptly announced on Saturday that he had offered White, whom he described as “a violent Fighter and Warrior”, the role of White House press secretary, which has been largely vacant since Karoline Leavitt departed the administration this summer. Leavitt initial replacement, Katie Zacharia, lasted five days in the job.

“Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other,” said Trump. “Dana, please take the job!”

After Trump also threatened Democrats planning to conduct oversight of his administration and family, announcing he had ordered the US Department of Justice to “look into” them, attorney general Todd Blanche told CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday that “there could be” investigations. Republicans have faced “dangerous” threats, Blanche claimed, without specifying what crimes he believed had been committed. “You have to draw the line.”

Democrats have made clear that Miller and Elon Musk, the world’s richest man and a close Trump ally, are likely to be targets of congressional investigations once the party retakes control of Congress in January.

Congressman Robert Garcia, a Democrat from California, who is set to chair the powerful oversight committee in the House of Representatives next year, said on Sunday that investigations are set to explore Musk’s involvement in the Department of Government Efficiency’s mass firing of federal workers last year, and Miller’s role in Trump’s immigration crackdown. “I think there’s a lot ⁠of interest – not just from our committee, but from committees across the Congress – to speak to Mr Musk,” Garcia told CNN.

Representative Jamie Raskin, poised to become the chair of the House judiciary committee, has also requested information on the business dealings of Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and son Donald Trump Jr.

With 33 of 35 Senate races called, the Democrats had won 54 seats to the Republicans’ 44. Votes are still being counted in Alaska, which had long been seen as a key battleground, and Mississippi, a previous Republican stronghold which remains too close to call.

Congressman James Comer, a Republican from Kentucky who currently heads the House oversight committee before his party cedes control to Democrats, told Fox News that the committee is going to dedicate the last two months of this congress investigating Alaska over the controversy surrounding its Senate race.

Trump has already threatened Democratic candidate Mary Peltola with criminal prosecution over reports that her campaign was linked to the recruitment of a second “Dan Sullivan” in Alaska’s Senate race, with the same name as the Republican candidate.

Democrats meanwhile embarked on a victory lap this weekend, celebrating their historic wins on Tuesday. Democratic candidates won after running on policies that would “change working peoples’ lives”, New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani told Fox News on Sunday.

“We are seeing a moment in time where working class Americans have made very clear that they are tired of waiting,” said Mamdani. “They are tired of being told, again and again, that there is less for them to make ends meet, while we see the world’s first trillionaire emerge in Elon Musk.”

But there has been friction within the party regarding the incoming congressional leadership, with Chuck Schumer set to become the next majority leader in the US Senate Hakeem Jeffries widely expected to become House speaker.

Senator-elect Adam Hamilton of Kansas – the first Democrat the state has sent to the US Senate in almost a century – told NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday the Schumer is a “kind of polarizing figure” adding: “It feels like it is a time for fresh and new ideas, and somebody who can unite us instead of dividing us.”

During a Saturday Night Live skit this weekend, a member of the cast impersonated Trump attacking James Talarico, the Democrat who ran for US Senate in Texas, and called him “Talafreako” – only for Talarico himself to walk out on stage.

“That’s senator Talafreako,” he said, to loud cheers, after becoming the first Democrat to win statewide office in Texas since 1994.

title: Gadi Eisenkot reaches out to Netanyahu allies as he strives to form government
excerpt:
Former military chief says prime minister brought Israel to historic crisis and it is approaching ‘point of no return’

Israel’s former military chief Gadi Eisenkot started the tough task of forming a...
body_text:
Former military chief says prime minister brought Israel to historic crisis and it is approaching ‘point of no return’

Israel’s former military chief Gadi Eisenkot started the tough task of forming a government on Sunday, reaching out to Benjamin Netanyahu’s allies as he said the veteran prime minister had brought the country to a historic crisis.

Eisenkot, 66, the leader of the Yashar party, who has vowed to bridge Israel’s deep polarisation under Netanyahu, formally received a mandate from the president, Isaac Herzog, who gave him 28 days to form a government despite his bloc lacking a clear majority.

“We are in a state of emergency, approaching a point of no return for the state of Israel,” said Eisenkot, who had traded his usual all black for a suit and tie at a ceremony at the presidential office. “We must form a national emergency government. This will require creative and unconventional political steps.”

Eisenkot faces significant challenges on the road to becoming prime minister. He has three options: a power-sharing agreement with Netanyahu, support from Arab-led parties – something several members of his bloc do not support – or an agreement with the ultra-Orthodox parties, which demand military exemptions for their community.

Eisenkot and Herzog acknowledged Israel’s growing isolation under Netanyahu, who is wanted by the international criminal court.

In the US, Israel’s closest ally, Democrats on Tuesday swept the midterm elections, with calls to rein in Israel after the devastation in Gaza and the unpopular Iran war, which Netanyahu launched with Donald Trump.

Eisenkot said: “We are in the midst of a devastating diplomatic crisis. Even our closest friends and strategic allies are saying their relationship with Israel must be reassessed.”

He appealed to Netanyahu’s Likud party as well as the far-right party of the finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, to join him – but only with himself as prime minister.

“My door is open and my hand is extended, wholeheartedly and willingly, to anyone who understands the gravity of this moment,” he said.

Should Eisenkot succeed in forming a coalition, he would take over as prime minister from Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving premier.

Eisenkot’s wide-ranging opposition bloc won 48 of the Israeli parliament’s 120 seats in the October elections, while Netanyahu’s camp secured 53, leaving neither with a majority.

During party consultations with Herzog, Eisenkot received the endorsements of both Arab-majority lists, who could now play kingmakers after making unprecedented gains in the vote.

Eisenkot has laid out a series of conditions for any Arab party to join his coalition, including recognition of Israel as a Jewish state and declaring the Palestinian militant group Hamas a terrorist organisation. One of his partners, the more conservative Yisrael Beiteinu party, has already said it will not join a coalition with Arab-led parties.

Eisenkot, a former army chief, and his partners made equal military service a central part of their campaign. Specifically, they are seeking an end to the longstanding draft exemptions enjoyed by the ultra-Orthodox.

Netanyahu has repeatedly claimed the election was “stolen” by Arab parties, which rallied their supporters to vote in large numbers. But he has offered little to no evidence to support the claims.

Netanyahu is expected to continue his pressure tactics against Eisenkot, saying any alliance with the Arab parties would be an act of betrayal.

Israel’s Shin Bet security agency has launched an investigation into possible foreign interference in the vote, but the country’s Central Elections Committee – and Herzog – say the vote was valid and even if wrongdoing was found, it did not have a significant impact on the result.

Netanyahu called for a “national unity” government with Eisenkot on Saturday night but it remains unclear whether the two rivals could agree on a power-sharing agreement. These types of coalition governments are notoriously fragile and often collapse.

Eisenkot, the military chief of staff from 2015 to 2019, has set out to unite Israelis after Netanyahu’s divisive tenure, under which the country moved sharply to the right.

He has vowed to crack down on extremist West Bank settlers who have attacked Palestinians with impunity, decrying recent incidents as “Jewish terror” abetted by Netanyahu’s government.

He opposes the creation of a Palestinian state and has vowed to end Hamas’s rule in Gaza and destroy the Islamist movement’s military wing.

Commanding the military during the 2006 war with Hezbollah, Eisenkot devised the so-called “Dahiya doctrine”. The idea, named after a Beirut suburb heavily damaged in that war, involves Israel vowing to use massive force against civilian infrastructure in areas controlled by the Lebanese militant movement Hezbollah.

After his appointment, Eisenkot will have 28 days to come up with the 61 votes needed for a government. If he comes up short, Herzog can provide a 14-day extension before he has to offer the mandate to someone else.

If neither side succeeds, Israel will head to fresh elections. The country held five elections between 2019 and 2022 owing to repeated deadlocks.

title: Labour expected to cut EV targets for UK’s car industry despite MPs’ protests
excerpt:
Exclusive: Louise Haigh likely to weaken mandate for sales that forms key part of emission reduction plan

Analysis: Climate always comes second – are green issues slipping down Burnham’s agenda?

Min...
body_text:
Exclusive: Louise Haigh likely to weaken mandate for sales that forms key part of emission reduction plan

Analysis: Climate always comes second – are green issues slipping down Burnham’s agenda?

Ministers are expected to make steep cuts to the government’s electric vehicle (EV) targets this week, in a move that will relieve carmakers but alarm many Labour MPs who are worried about the government’s commitment to the green agenda.

Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, will finalise the plan after a crunch meeting in Downing Street on Wednesday to settle a long-running dispute between the transport, energy and business departments.

Haigh is expected to agree to cut a target for EV sales by about a quarter, government sources say, helping British industry but setting up a potential fight with MPs and campaigners over the government’s single biggest decarbonisation policy.

The decision will be made just as Andy Burnham prepares to travel to his first Cop summit as prime minister, where he and the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, will champion electrification on a global scale.

With some MPs already upset by the decisions to approve the Jackdaw gasfield and to cut funding for green schemes to pay for higher defence spending, many see the upcoming decisions on the Rosebank oilfield and the EV mandate as critically important.

Lizzi Collinge, the Labour MP for Morecambe and Lunesdale, said: “The upcoming decision on the ZEV [zero emission vehicle] mandate will have a huge climate impact, possibly the biggest one that’s on the PM’s desk.

“But it will also set the direction for tackling the cost of living and helping get our energy prices down over the coming decade.”

Catherine Fookes, the MP for Monmouthshire, said: “The government has some incredibly difficult decisions to make in the coming months and the prime minister will need to weigh up the consequences of each. We need the ZEV mandate to stay, and Rosebank to be rejected.”

A government spokesperson said: “The government is united in its commitment to the ZEV mandate and no decisions have been taken.

“We are committed to the phaseout of all new cars relying solely on petrol and diesel engines by 2030, and to 100% of new car and van sales being zero emission by 2035, and our legally binding net zero targets.

“Our consultation on the mandate will not change this, and will ensure we are taking a pragmatic and balanced approach to the ZEV transition.”

Under rules brought in by the last Conservative government, carmakers have to make sure they only sell EVs by 2035, gradually increasing the proportion over time to 80% by 2030.

The policy is expected to create greater emissions savings than any other, leading to nearly 14% of all the reductions to which the UK has pledged between 2028 and 2032.

Carmakers have warned for years, however, that the interim targets in particular are unattainable, arguing that higher inflation and a squeeze on living standards have pushed them out of reach.

The Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) says the industry will miss this year’s 33% target by a wide margin, with battery EVs accounting for 26.6% of new car sales in the first 10 months of the year.

Those targets, however, do not take into account exemptions that allow carmakers to avoid fines even if they undershoot their targets, such as by selling more hybrid cars, or making up for lower sales of electric cars now by selling more in the future.

Mike Hawes, the SMMT’s chief executive, said: “The gap between demand and mandated targets continues to widen.

“Meaningful change to the trajectory, alongside expanded flexibilities throughout the regulation, is essential to bridge that gap, safeguard jobs and investment while keeping the UK’s zero emission transition on track.”

With ministers already having diluted the targets on multiple occasions since the policy was first proposed, the government launched another review into the policy in August, proposing five main options.

They were: to keep the mandate unchanged; keep it at 80% but extend the flexibilities by four years to 2034; reduce the interim target to 70%; reduce it to 60%; or reduce it to 50%.

That consultation kickstarted an internal battle in Whitehall. Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, has argued for the 2030 target to be reduced as far as possible, to 50%.

Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, is believed to want it to be approximately 60%, while Miatta Fahnbulleh and her predecessor as energy secretary, Ed Miliband, are understood to want it to remain at 80%.

The prime minister would normally have sought to have resolved the dispute, but Burnham has recused himself from the decision because his wife, Marie-France van Heel, advises the board of the Manchester-based electric vehicle charging network Be.EV.

Government insiders say Haigh will probably sign off on a 2030 target of about 60%, while also extending the flexibilities in the targets until 2034. She is understood to have told colleagues, however, that she does not want them to come back in the future demanding another target reduction.

The decision will not only upset some Labour MPs, it will also dismay people in the wider environmental movement and in the EV charging industry, which is relying on high vehicle sales to recoup investment.

Shane Brennan, the chief executive of the trade association ChargeUK, said: “Weakening the mandate puts £1.7bn of charging infrastructure at risk and all the associated jobs and supply chain spending that goes with it.

“Charging investors’ confidence will be rocked by a third change in three years. Government should be in no way complacent about the long-term implications of being seen to cave to the short-term interest of global car importers.”

Paul McNamee, the director of the Labour Climate and Environment Forum, said: “Significant weakening of the ZEV mandate from the current 80% targets will be seen as a rowing back on climate leadership.

“If the government does this, it must provide assurance that the mandate will not be weakened again in the coming years, the 2035 target for EVs remains in place, and it delivers a robust industrial strategy to build a strong EV manufacturing base in the UK that will protect jobs in the long term.”

title: Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least seven
excerpt:
President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 30 miles from Cairo

Seven people were killed and more than 100 injured when two trains collided on Sunday ...
body_text:
President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 30 miles from Cairo

Seven people were killed and more than 100 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said.

The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 30 miles south of Cairo, when a train travelling to Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry.

An inspection indicated that the Cairo-Aswan train had been stationary on the same track, officials said.

Train derailments and crashes are common in Egypt, where the railway system has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance of equipment. In recent years the government has announced modernisation initiatives to improve its railways.

Ayman Gamal, a resident of Kafr Girza in al-Ayyat where the crash occurred, said people rushed to the scene, pulled out survivors and called ambulances.

Gamal said he saw about 80 of the injured being taken by ambulances to hospital. He said some passengers were trapped inside one of the carriages of the stationary train and died.

Egypt’s president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said in a social media post that he had ordered a prompt investigation.

Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the scene to clear the wreckage and restore train services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian railway authority said.

Last September, a train driver and his assistant were injured after two freight trains collided in the same district.

Egypt’s deadliest train crash was in 2002 when more than 300 people were killed after a fire broke out on an overnight train journeying from Cairo to southern Egypt.

title: Hundreds of thousands join Amsterdam’s ‘Red Line’ protest against Israel
excerpt: More than 200,000 people have taken to the streets of Amsterdam in the Netherlands, demanding government action against Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, according to the Dutch branch of Amnesty Interna...
body_text:
More than 200,000 people have taken to the streets of Amsterdam in the Netherlands, demanding government action against Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, according to the Dutch branch of Amnesty International, one of the organisers.

Sunday’s ‘Red Line’ protesters, many wearing red items of clothing, called for tighter trade restrictions on Israel and a halt to all arms sales.

“What is happening there is inhumane,” Mike van Dongen said as he walked in the huge throng of people.

“As far as I’m concerned, [the Dutch authorities] are doing nothing,” he said. “They don’t dare take any serious steps.”

As the protesters marched along a normally busy Amsterdam street that was closed to traffic on Sunday, a man stood at a bus stop with a loudspeaker shouting, “Free, free Palestine!” Many of the marchers echoed his cry as they passed.

Israel’s genocidal war has killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, including 21,000 children, since October 2023.

Sunday’s protest was similar to one in early October last year. That followed ‘Red Line’ demonstrations last June when protesters marched through the streets of The Hague.

A “ceasefire” took effect in Gaza on October 10 last year, but Israeli attacks and killings have continued on an almost-daily basis since.

The war in Gaza has strained relations between the Netherlands and Israel. The Dutch foreign minister resigned last year after failing to secure new sanctions against Israel.

Since then, a new minority coalition government took power in February and introduced an import ban on products from Israeli settlements, which the Dutch government and most of the international community consider illegal – the ban provoked a diplomatic spat with Israel.

Prime Minister Rob Jetten, who took part in a march last year but was not present on Sunday, defended his government’s actions at his weekly news conference on Friday.

“Every single day and every single week, we do what we can to alleviate the terrible situation there,” he said.

He added that his administration is “exerting greater political and diplomatic pressure” on Israel to abide by its agreements on Gaza.

title: Half of NHS trusts in England lack funds earmarked to cover maternity leave
excerpt:
Physiotherapy services hit particularly hard compared with other areas of healthcare such as nursing, union finds

Almost half of the NHS trusts in England have no earmarked funding to cover staff on ...
body_text:
Physiotherapy services hit particularly hard compared with other areas of healthcare such as nursing, union finds

Almost half of the NHS trusts in England have no earmarked funding to cover staff on maternity leave, according to analysis that raises fresh concerns about pressure on physiotherapy services.

Freedom of information requests sent to the trusts by the Chartered Society of Physiotherapy (CSP) found that 49% had neither a dedicated budget nor a policy to permit overspending to pay for maternity cover.

Where funding does exist, the analysis revealed that physiotherapy appears to be treated less favourably than other areas of healthcare. More than one in five trusts (22%) said their maternity cover arrangements did not extend to physiotherapy staff, compared with only 9% for nursing posts.

The CSP said failing to plan for maternity leave risked leaving overstretched teams to shoulder the same workload with fewer people, meaning patients waiting longer for treatment and rehabilitation. The findings are also especially stark given that women make up about 79% of the NHS physiotherapy workforce.

The CSP’s director of practice and development, Ash James, said it was deeply concerning that physiotherapy teams were significantly less likely than their nursing colleagues to have access to funding for maternity cover.

“When a physiotherapist goes on maternity leave, the patients needing treatment don’t disappear. Without cover, already overstretched colleagues are left trying to absorb the workload, potentially leaving patients waiting longer for the rehabilitation they need,” he said.

“This is happening against a backdrop of recruitment freezes, disappearing posts and growing demand for care. It is yet another example of physiotherapy services being stretched beyond their capacity. Trusts must ensure maternity cover arrangements are available fairly across clinical professions, while the government must urgently lift recruitment freezes and invest in the physiotherapy workforce.”

Earlier research suggested that stroke patients and others who need intensive physiotherapy were receiving poorer care because hospitals lacked adequate space and equipment.

That research found four out of 10 NHS physiotherapy staff had lost or expected to lose dedicated rehabilitation space. In a survey of more than 2,000 members by the CSP, six out of 10 said their rooms had been taken over by other clinical teams, with some blaming a lack of funding or managers who did not prioritise their work.

The body is calling for equal access to maternity cover funding across NHS professions as well as urgent action on recruitment freezes and staff shortages in physiotherapy.

The chair of the Patients’ Association, Alastair Henderson, said the gaps in cover had direct consequences for patients. “When services are already stretched, losing staff without adequate replacement can mean longer waits for treatment and rehabilitation, less access to specialist expertise and greater pressure on remaining teams,” he said.

“Patients should not have to wait longer or miss out on the care they need because the NHS has failed to plan for or cannot afford to cover predictable staff absences.”

title: Seven dead and more than 100 injured after trains collide in Egypt
excerpt:
Footage shows derailed train carriages near Giza in Egypt

At least seven people have died in a train crash near the Egyptian city of Giza, with more than 100 injured.

The country's railway authority...
body_text:
Footage shows derailed train carriages near Giza in Egypt

At least seven people have died in a train crash near the Egyptian city of Giza, with more than 100 injured.

The country's railway authority said two trains travelling south from Giza and Cairo collided, causing several carriages to derail and fall down an embankment.

Images from the scene showed people looking inside overturned carriages for injured passengers as a massive emergency response was launched.

Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said he had ordered state authorities to "investigate the circumstances of the accident, and hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent".

The public prosecutor's office warned the death toll could rise.

Uninjured passengers and passersby searched derailed carriages for injured people

The government said hospitals in the area had been put "on heightened alert" as they dealt with a massive influx of patients.

Egypt's health minister Dr Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said people were being treated for broken bones and head injuries.

The driver of one of the trains was among those who died in the crash, the ministry confirmed.

The first train involved in the crash was travelling from Giza to Fayoum, south of Cairo, when it crashed into the rear of another service heading south from Cairo to Aswan, which was stationary on the tracks.

Images from the scene showed some carriages had overturned, with the body of at least one appearing to have split in two.

Trains between Giza and the Upper Egypt region were suspended as cranes were dispatched to remove the wrecked trains.

The collision occurred in the area between Kafr Ammar and Al-Raqqa stations in Al-Ayyat, close to where Egypt's deadliest train tragedy occurred in February 2002, when a fire engulfed a passenger train travelling from Cairo to Luxor.

The train continued for around nine kilometres (5.6 miles) before coming to a halt.

In that incident, more than 370 people were officially reported killed, although some estimates put the toll considerably higher.

Two further crashes in the area in 2009 killed dozens more.

There were calls in Egypt on Sunday for the transport minister to resign over the latest deadly rail disaster.

title: The week of the backup QB in the NFL kicks off as Sanders, Milton, Minshew, Lock, and Wentz start
excerpt: The Los Angeles Chargers are 0-7, and Nick Wright has called them the "biggest disappointment in NFL history." Chris Broussard and Kevin Wildes discuss this take and ask if it’s valid, and they discus...
body_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers are 0-7, and Nick Wright has called them the "biggest disappointment in NFL history." Chris Broussard and Kevin Wildes discuss this take and ask if it’s valid, and they discuss Shedeur Sanders being in line to start for the Cleveland Browns as Deshaun Watson is in concussion protocol.

It is the week of the backup quarterback around the NFL and by the time we're done, we could come to understand why the quarterback-driven league is, for some teams, a backup-quarterback-driven week.

Five backup quarterbacks are starting for their teams in Week 9, with three of those players thrust into the starting job on teams with playoff expectations.

MINNESOTA VIKINGS' SOFT BENCHING OF KYLER MURRAY LEADS TO CARSON WENTZ TAKING OVER AS NEW STARTING QB

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Arizona Cardinals quarterback Gardner Minshew II is sacked by Dallas Cowboys linebacker Tyrus Wheat and defensive tackle Lt. Overton in the first half at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Ariz., on Aug. 22, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

This is the week Shedeur Sanders starts for Deshaun Watson with the Cleveland Browns, Drew Lock starts instead of Sam Darnold for the Seattle Seahawks, Carson Wentz starts for Kyler Murray with the Minnesota Vikings – all playing on teams in thick of a playoff hunt.

The situation is probably different for the Arizona Cardinals, who are starting Gardner Minshew, and the Philadelphia Eagles, who are turning to Joe Milton because both those teams are currently outside the playoff picture and indeed under .500.

So here's the breakdown of five new starters and what is at stake:

Minshew's last start before this week was Oct. 6, 2024, with the Raiders, and unlike most of the others in this group, he has already been given a chance to extend his tenure beyond this game.

Tanner McKee and Joe Milton of the Philadelphia Eagles look on before the game against the Carolina Panthers at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, Pa., on Oct. 18, 2026. (Getty Images)

EAGLES' JALEN HURTS PLACED ON INJURED RESERVE AFTER SUPERFICIAL BLOOD CLOT FOUND IN HIS CALF AREA

This will be Milton’s first NFL start, and while the Eagles have not committed beyond this game, Hurts’ season-ending injury gives Milton a legitimate opportunity to keep the job if he plays well.

Minnesota Vikings quarterback Carson Wentz (11) drops back to pass against the Los Angeles Chargers during the first half at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California, on Oct. 23, 2025. (Gary A. Vasquez/Imagn Images)

Lock’s most recent start was Sept. 20 against Arizona, when he threw for 235 yards and three touchdowns. Darnold is expected to reclaim the job when healthy.

Cleveland Browns quarterback Shedeur Sanders throws a pass to tight end Carsen Ryan during the first half against the Buffalo Bills at Huntington Bank Field in Cleveland, Ohio, on Aug. 22, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

Sanders last started an NFL regular season game on Jan. 4, 2026, in the Browns’ 20-18 victory over Cincinnati, the seventh of his 2025 rookie season.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Sanders is not expected to take the starting job from Watson although playing well opens the door for him to be considered more of an option if Watson suddenly reverts to the type of play that made him something of an enigma in Cleveland before the 2026 season.

The biggest opportunity of the week is sitting there for Wentz. He has thrown 5 TD passes in 101 snaps for the Vikings this year.

Murray, meanwhile, has been inconsistent and thrown 6 TDs in over 300 snaps.

FOLLOW ARMANDO SALGUERO ON X: @ARMANDOSALGUERO

Armando Salguero is OutKick's Senior NFL Writer.

body_text:
Country music star Terri Clark tells OutKick OutDoors how fishing helps her unwind, shares her favorite moments on the water and laughs about practicing fishing knots on her tour bus.

Deer facing off with one another and settling matters physically isn't reserved for just the bucks during rutting season. Female deer will throw down too, especially if they feel the need to protect their young.

Back in September, this was on display in an amateur photographer's backyard. She heard noises coming from the yard and when she looked out of her window she saw two does going at it.

Stock image of two deer stand in a backyard. (Getty Images)

She grabbed her phone and captured a viral video. They weren't cracking skulls like the males do when they tangle antlers, they were on their hind legs using their front hooves to deliver blows.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

These ladies were absolutely letting them fly with combinations that a boxer would be proud of.

Stock image of two deer fighting on their hind legs. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)

"This happened in my yard yesterday evening," the woman who recorded the action wrote. "I was upstairs when I heard this noise outside like thumping, bumping and thrashing. My window was open so I ran towards it and saw these two deer fighting. Both were females protecting their young ones I think."

She added, "First time I have witnessed that. WOW! I immediately ran for my cell and started to video it through my mesh screen so hope it’s okay to view. The wildlife I see in my yard. Always thrilling."

YOUNG BUCK GETS RAGDOLLED AND TOSSED IN THE AIR DURING BATTLE WITH LARGER BUCK CAUGHT ON TRAIL CAM

A mesh screen isn't ideal for recording video, but it doesn't interfere at all with this action. The two go at it as a couple of fawns look on.

After several exchanges, one of them decides they've had enough. A valiant effort by both of the deer.

They will live to fight another day, although one of them is going to enter their next scrap with a little more confidence than the other. That's life. You win some and you lose some.

title: Leavitt reveals what Republicans must do to survive politically after Trump leaves White House
excerpt: Fox News contributor Karoline Leavitt shares what voters can take away from midterm elections to ensure a similar outcome doesn't happen again and offers advice to the next press secretary on 'My View...
body_text:
Fox News contributor Karoline Leavitt shares what voters can take away from midterm elections to ensure a similar outcome doesn't happen again and offers advice to the next press secretary on 'My View with Lara Trump.'

Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said Saturday that Republicans must find a new leader capable of connecting with working-class Americans and rebuilding President Donald Trump's political coalition once he leaves the White House.

"President Trump wasn't on the ballot in these midterms. He'll never be at the top of the ticket again, and I think we need somebody who is America first, who can really tap into the forgotten men and women that President Trump drew to the Republican Party in historic way from 2016 all the way through 2024," Leavitt said on "My View with Lara Trump"

Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt says the GOP must find a new leader who can connect with working Americans and carry Donald Trump's America First agenda. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

"You need someone who can really get out, speak to people about their struggles, their challenges, relate to them and offer promise and hope," she added, acknowledging that Democrats successfully motivated voters during the midterm elections.

Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections, capturing battleground Senate seats in Michigan, Texas, South Carolina, North Carolina, Maine and Minnesota while flipping key House seats in Virginia, Iowa and Nebraska.

MAGA VOTERS REVEAL WHO THEY WANT TO SEE LEAD GOP IN 2028

The former press secretary said the GOP's next leader must relate to working Americans' struggles and offer hope. (Evan Vucci/AP)

Leavitt urged Republicans to study their election losses and analyze individual races to determine how to correct course.

"I think that's something Democrats did well in this election, in the midterms, was they obviously inspired people to turn out to vote because they made the people feel like we're going to make your lives better," she said.

ELAINE PARKER: DEMOCRAT WIN IS A WAKE-UP CALL FOR REPUBLICANS, NOT A VOTE FOR SOCIALISM

"We need to do that again the same way, the same fashion President Trump did. It just has to be a new person at the top of the ticket."

Leavitt also reflected fondly on her time as White House press secretary, expressing gratitude for the experience. She said she has no plans to run for office, preferring to spend time at home with her young children.

"I'm so happy being with my kids. I have zero plans to run for office," she said. "I'm all set."

Max Bacall is an associate editor for Fox News Digital covering media, culture and comedy.

title: Russian strikes on Ukraine leave hundreds of thousands without electricity
excerpt:
More than 600,000 people in Ukraine’s eastern Dnipropetrovsk region are without electricity after a Russian overnight attack on an energy facility, a Ukrainian energy provider has said.

Residents acr...
body_text:
More than 600,000 people in Ukraine’s eastern Dnipropetrovsk region are without electricity after a Russian overnight attack on an energy facility, a Ukrainian energy provider has said.

Residents across the Pavlohrad, Samarivskyi, Kamianske and Dnipro districts, as well as the city of Dnipro, faced electricity outages on Sunday, power company DTEK wrote in a Telegram post.

Engineers were at the scene attempting to restore the damaged facility, but “repairs are being complicated by repeated attacks”, DTEK said.

Ukraine is bracing for yet another harsh winter of war as Russia ramps up daily aerial attacks, raining down drones and missiles on the power network.

Another 250,000 Ukrainians were left without power in the Kharkiv region in northeastern Ukraine on Sunday after Russia struck an infrastructure facility there.

“No casualties have been reported, ” said Mykola Baksheyev, mayor of Zlatopil city, on Telegram.

“Power engineers are currently working to repair the damage; however, the exact timeframe for restoring the electricity supply remains unknown.”

The attacks came a day after Ukraine’s Ministry of Energy said a massive attack on energy facilities had plunged residents in five regions into darkness and significantly hampered electricity transmission in Kyiv.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of intensifying attacks to put pressure on Kyiv at United States-brokered trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday.

Russia’s Ministry of Defence stated on its Telegram channel that its forces will “continue to carry out strikes against Ukrainian fuel and energy infrastructure facilities” that they say are used to aid the Ukrainian military.

title: Gulf War veteran left homeless after heart surgery details how he rebuilt his life from 'square one'
excerpt: U.S.VETS Executive Director Quandrea Patterson and veteran Thomas Garrett Jr. join 'Fox News Live' to highlight the 'Make Camo Your Cause' campaign. Garret discusses the challenges of transitioning to...
body_text:
U.S.VETS Executive Director Quandrea Patterson and veteran Thomas Garrett Jr. join 'Fox News Live' to highlight the 'Make Camo Your Cause' campaign. Garret discusses the challenges of transitioning to civilian life after returning from the Gulf War.

Gulf War veteran Thomas Garrett Jr. returned home to celebratory parades, but years later, he found himself homeless after undergoing heart surgery.

Garrett’s efforts to rebuild his life after becoming homeless are highlighted in Fox Corporation’s sixth annual "Make Camo Your Cause" campaign with U.S.VETS, a nationwide initiative ahead of Veterans Day aimed at helping end veteran homelessness.

"The homecoming was a phenomenal event," Garrett said Saturday on "Fox News Live."

"I became homeless after having heart surgery. So that changed everything about my dynamic in life," he added.

AMERICA'S WOUNDED, STRUGGLING VETERANS GET BRAND-NEW HOMES BUILT BY FLORIDA TEENS

Gulf War veteran Thomas Garrett Jr. appears on "Fox News Live" on Saturday to discuss his experience with homelessness following heart surgery and his journey toward rebuilding his life. (Screenshot/"Fox News Live")

U.S.VETS, a national nonprofit dedicated to ending veteran homelessness, provides housing, food and career help to service members in need. According to the organization, it assists more than 20,000 veterans and their families each year. To date, U.S.VETS has served over 500,000 meals, provided 418,000 nights of shelter and placed 3,000 veterans into permanent housing.

Quandrea Patterson, executive director of U.S.VETS, explained that Garrett’s experience reflects a broader challenge facing veterans as they transition from military to civilian life.

NEW YORK JETS OWNER WOODY JOHNSON TO BE HONORED AT TUNNEL TO TOWERS GALA FOR DECADE-LONG PARTNERSHIP

U.S.VETS executive director Quandrea Patterson appears on "Fox News Live" on Saturday to discuss the challenges veterans face when transitioning from military to civilian life, including the risk of homelessness. (Screenshot/"Fox News Live")

"A lot of times when veterans are in service, they're told, and they know exactly what to do because they're mission-focused," Patterson said. "And then during that transition from active service to civilian service or veteran status, a lot of the information, a lot of the things to expect are unknown."

The uncertainty surrounding that transition can leave veterans vulnerable to homelessness, Patterson said.

For Garrett, U.S.VETS offered the structure and support he needed to move forward.

"U.S.VETS is a new starting point for veterans," Garrett said. "It's a square one to where you can build up your life the way the veteran themselves need it. It gives us good structure. It gives us a good routine to begin and to build from there."

TRUMP PROMOTES FREEDOM HAULERS INITIATIVE TO FAST-TRACK MILITARY VETERANS INTO TRUCKING JOBS

Ahead of Veterans Day, Patterson stressed that honoring those who served requires more than celebrating them once a year.

"Freedom isn’t free, and for the freedom that we're experiencing, that, there is somebody out there volunteering to put their life on the line and to navigate the unknown," Patterson said. "When they get out, we should wrap our arms around them to make sure that they know that that service was appreciated in more than just words, but in deed as well."

ARMY VET, TRUCKING EXECUTIVE RAVES OVER TRUMP PLAN TO BOLSTER BLUE COLLAR INDUSTRY BY FAST-TRACKING VETERANS

Fox Corporation's sixth annual "Make Camo Your Cause" campaign is in partnership with U.S.VETS. The initiative aims to raise awareness and funds to help combat veteran homelessness across the United States. (Screenshot/"Fox News Live")

FOX SPORTS TO HONOR MILITARY AHEAD OF VETERANS DAY WITH TWO-DAY SALUTE DURING COLLEGE FOOTBALL, NFL COVERAGE

FOX is the founding media sponsor of the campaign, which aims to bring visibility and awareness to the tragic issue in the United States while transforming what it means to wear camo here at home.

Over the past five years, the campaign has driven significant donations to U.S.VETS and greater awareness of the critical work it does.

Viewers can "Make Camo Your Cause" by donating or shopping online at the link.

Fox News Digital’s Brian Flood contributed to this report.

Madison Colombo is a writer for Fox News Digital’s Flash, Media, and Culture team, covering daily breaking news and trending topics with an award-winning background in broadcast and digital journalism.

title: UK spent £100m on zombie Brexit border inspection posts
excerpt:
Five of seven facilities in England and Wales never reached operational stage as Tories vacillated over plans to check goods

The UK wasted at least £100m in taxpayers’ money to set up zombie Brexit b...
body_text:
Five of seven facilities in England and Wales never reached operational stage as Tories vacillated over plans to check goods

The UK wasted at least £100m in taxpayers’ money to set up zombie Brexit border inspection posts that were never used, it has been revealed.

The overall cost of Brexit was put at an estimated £4.7bn by the National Audit Office last year but this included years-long transformation of the software used for customs declarations and other systems built to cope with the UK leaving the single market.

Now fresh information from HMRC on the exact spend on the seven “inland border facilities” has come to light. The sites were built but quickly decommissioned as the Conservative government at the time vacillated over plans to check goods coming in from the continent.

Five of the seven “inland border facilities” in England and Wales never got to operational stage because the Tories decided not to implement all the border checks after concluding food coming from the EU would be the same high standard as it was before Brexit.

Portsmouth port, which is owned by the city council, spent £23m on building its border control post, which has never been used at full capacity because of the decision to scale back the checks.

The port received £17.1m in government funding for the project, leaving the council to make up the £6m shortfall, which could otherwise have been spent on essential services.

The EU launched all the checks in Calais, Dublin and other European ports from day one as the UK was treated as a “third country” overnight. The most controversial British zombie facility was known as “Dover white cliffs”. Furious residents at the village of Guston were told of the plans for the inland border facility on 31 December 2020, just hours before a “transition year” ended and Brexit was due to be implemented with supposed checks on all lorries coming across the Channel.

Information from HMRC, released under a freedom of information request, shows the facility has so far cost the taxpayer £28m, even though it remains a field. The Department for Transport paid £21m to procure the site and spent a further £7m on initial ground works, including an archaeological survey for any roman remains.

Another £17m was spent on a border facility in Birmingham planned at the airport car park. Newly released information shows it cost £11m to build with £6m in “closure costs”.

Another £20m was spent on sites in Warrington and in Ebbsfleet, a town just south of the Dartford Bridge on the Thames estuary. The Warrington site, on the former Shearings holidays coach stop at Appleton Thorn, was chosen because there were no suitable sites available for lorries coming from Ireland into Liverpool, Holyhead and Heysham ports.

Local people vehemently opposed the site at the time. It cost £7m to buy, £9m to build and £1m to decommission.

Another £10m was spent preparing customs and other checks at the former car park at Eurostar Ebbsfleet International train station, which cost £4m to convert into a lorry park and £6m to close, according to HMRC data.

A further £5m was spent on another site tucked away off the M11, just south of Stansted, at North Weald airfield. This airfield was commandeered for the same purpose, to avert congestion on the M25. It cost £3m to build and £2m to close down.

HMRC said Birmingham, Ebbsfleet and North Weald “did not require the acquisition of land”. The decision to build Brexit lorry parks so far from Dover underlined the lack of preparation for the UK’s departure from the EU.

Most of the UK’s lorry traffic is concentrated in Dover, but as a designated area of outstanding beauty it was impossible to conduct the post-Brexit customs and standard checks near the port.

The UK finally opted for a site 20 miles inland at Sevington in Kent, but even that was last minute. The government previously revealed in a parliamentary question that total capital costs ran to £154m.

This included £30m on the acquisition of farmland between Sevington and Mersham for Britain’s principal Brexit border facility and another £70m to build.

HMRC has revealed through freedom of information that the operational costs have run to £179m, money that would not have been spent had Brexit not happened.

The second site that remains operational is Holyhead – a small site close to the main road to the port which receives goods from Ireland. According to the FoI, the site cost £14m to acquire and another £23m to build.

The figures are separate to investments made by Eurotunnel, the Port of Dover and other ports including Portsmouth. Eurotunnel spent €50m (£41.7m) on building the infrastructure for Brexit checks for trucks and €90m on changes for passengers, including an entry and exit system that has never been activated by the French.

The £23m border control post at Portsmouth, the UK’s second-busiest cross-Channel port, now faces an uncertain future. The hi-tech facility was built to government specifications to handle post-Brexit checks. Two trailer checks take place on average each day, according to the port’s director, Mike Sellers, compared with the 80 checks originally envisioned.

He said: “Given the border post’s location within the operational port, ideally we would look to repurpose it rather than demolish it, but it will cost us almost as much to repurpose as to demolish. It was bespoke and built for food import checks and biosecurity, it is not suitable for general warehousing and will have to be changed.”

Sellers and Portsmouth city council’s leader are among the ports calling on the government to provide compensation for the border posts that will become redundant when the UK government’s deal with the EU comes into force.

title: At least 21 dead as small boat sinks off Senegal
excerpt:

The Senegalese Interior Ministry said in a statement on Sunday that one person had been resc...
body_text:
A small boat carrying migrants and refugees has sunk off northwestern Senegal, killing at least 21 people.

The Senegalese Interior Ministry said in a statement on Sunday that one person had been rescued in addition to the 21 bodies recovered.

The ministry said the death toll was “provisional” as of late Saturday, adding that the search was still ongoing and the families of the victims were being helped.

Media reports said the pirogue-type flat-bottomed boat capsized on Saturday off the Loumpoul dunes in the Kebemer department, between Dakar and the northern city of Saint-Louis.

Le Soleil newspaper said that most of the victims were from the Leona and Thieppe districts in the same department.

Spanish authorities on the Canary Island of El Hierro declared an emergency on Saturday after a surge in migrant boat arrivals. Since the start of November, El Hierro authorities said more than 3,300 people had arrived aboard around 30 boats.

title: Blue Angels pilot removed from team for 'failing to uphold' standards, Navy says
excerpt:
The U.S. Navy Blue Angels conducted a flyover above a beach in Pensacola, Florida, on Wednesday, as beachgoers cheered. (Partridge Drones via Facebook)

A Blue Angels pilot was removed from the Navy’s...
body_text:
The U.S. Navy Blue Angels conducted a flyover above a beach in Pensacola, Florida, on Wednesday, as beachgoers cheered. (Partridge Drones via Facebook)

A Blue Angels pilot was removed from the Navy’s flight demonstration team for "failing to uphold" its standards, leaving squadron with a five-jet show on Friday.

The dismissal comes just months after a controversial low Pensacola Beach flyover in July that sent debris flying, raising concern for public safety.

Maj. Scott Laux, a second-year member of the elite team, was identified as Blue Angel No. 6. The Chief of Naval Air Training (CNATRA) confirmed his removal to the Pensacola News Journal, saying the decision was announced Friday before the season finale at home in Pensacola.

NAVY SAYS NO REPRIMANDS OR FIRINGS AFTER BLUE ANGELS’ LOW PASS OVER BEACHGOERS

Blue Angels #6 opposing solo Maj. Scott Laux, USMC, answers media questions at NAS Pensacola on July 16, 2026 after the controversial low beach flyover.

"Blue Angel #6 was removed from the team for failing to uphold the standards expected of members of the Navy Flight Demonstration Squadron and will not participate in the team’s remaining performance this season," CNATRA’s public affairs office wrote in a statement Friday.

Fox News Digital reached out for further information Sunday morning and has not yet heard back.

Laux previously defended the team’s low-flying displays after the July flyover over Pensacola Beach sent tents, beach chairs and umbrellas flying as sand swept across the shoreline.

"We appreciate the trust in support and it’s our privilege to be able to perform in that way," Laux told Rolling with Madrina after the incident. "We’re gonna keep bringing the heat and continue doing it safely."

VIRAL VIDEO OF JETS BUZZING DHL STADIUM IN CAPE TOWN PROMPTS AVIATION SAFETY INVESTIGATION

Maj. Scott Laux spent one year as a narrator and most of his second year on the Blue Angels as opposing solo #6, before being shelved before the final performance of the season this weekend. (Getty Images)

Navy and War Department leaders had previously defended the low flyovers.

"Flight debrief complete. No reprimands. No firings. No problem," Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao wrote on X in July. "That’s the sound of Freedom! Semper fi and Hooyah."

War Secretary Pete Hegseth had vowed more support.

"The flyovers will continue until morale improves," Hegseth wrote on X.

The White House posted a photo meme of the controversial flyover from its official X account.

"It's okay to love America," the post read.

HEGSETH STEPS IN TO ‘FIX’ SITUATION AFTER APACHE PILOTS SUSPENDED FOR ‘SALUTE FROM THE SHORES’ FLYOVER

Marine Corps Maj. Scott Laux was outspoken in defending the July low beach flyover, but he is the one who has conspicuously been removed from the Blue Angels' final performance of the season. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

The Navy has not said when Laux was dismissed or what conduct prompted the decision. His photo and biography are no longer featured on the Blue Angels’ website's team page

Laux was absent from the squadron’s NAS Pensacola Homecoming Air Show on Friday and Saturday, where the team performed with five jets instead of its usual six. Laux's role was the opposing solo, which flies with lead solo #5 in the head-on crossing passes and mirror-image maneuvers that fill the gaps between the four-jet Diamond’s routines.

The routines were adjusted to account for the missing jet, according to reports.

The 2026 narrator, Lt. Commander Ronny Hafeza, might replace Laux on the 2027 team. The Blue Angels officers serve three-year terms, one as a narrator as Laux did.

Laux, a native of Chantilly, Va., graduated from the U.S. Naval Academy in 2012 with a degree in Chinese and earned his wings in 2015, according to his bio, which as of Sunday morning could still be accessed on the site despite no longer being listed with the rest of the team. He flew F/A-18 Hornets with Marine Corps squadrons, deployed to Japan and aboard the USS Nimitz and supported three operations during the 2020 carrier deployment: Resolute Support, Inherent Resolve and Octave Quartz.

A Blue Angels jet conducts a low pass over Pensacola Beach on Wednesday. (Partridge Drones via Facebook)

The Navy’s Blue Angels fly in formation over Pensacola Beach. (Stephen Lashbrook)

People gathered at Pensacola Beach to photograph and video Blue Angels jets conducting a flyover on Wednesday. (Partridge Drones via Facebook)

The Blue Angels take to the skies during a flight over Florida’s Gulf Coast on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. (Stephen Lashbrook)

The U.S. Navy Blue Angels fly over Pensacola Beach on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. (Stephen Lashbrook)

The U.S. Navy Blue Angels fly over a pier along the Pensacola Beach coastline on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. (Stephen Lashbrook)

The Blue Angels soar above the Florida coastline during a Wednesday flight. (Stephen Lashbrook)

Video shared online showed beachgoers cheering as a Blue Angels jet made a low pass over Pensacola Beach on Wednesday. (Partridge Drones via Facebook)

Video shared online showed beachgoers cheering as two Blue Angels jets made a low pass over Pensacola Beach on Wednesday. (Partridge Drones via Facebook)

He later transitioned to the F-35C Lightning II and served as an instructor pilot before joining the Blue Angels in September 2024. Before becoming Blue Angels #6, he served as the show's narrator.

Laux has more than 1,300 flight hours and 169 aircraft carrier landings. His awards include two Navy and Marine Corps Commendation Medals and multiple unit awards.

Eric Mack is a breaking news reporter and writer Sunday through Thursday, 6 a.m. ET to 2 p.m. ET, with a particular interest in stories that lead the news cycle on politics, elections, foreign affairs and government.

title: Blue Angels pilot removed from team for 'failing to uphold' standards, Navy says
excerpt:
The U.S. Navy Blue Angels conducted a flyover above a beach in Pensacola, Florida, on Wednesday, as beachgoers cheered. (Partridge Drones via Facebook)

A Blue Angels pilot was removed from the Navy’s...
body_text:
The U.S. Navy Blue Angels conducted a flyover above a beach in Pensacola, Florida, on Wednesday, as beachgoers cheered. (Partridge Drones via Facebook)

A Blue Angels pilot was removed from the Navy’s flight demonstration team for "failing to uphold" its standards, leaving squadron with a five-jet show on Friday.

The dismissal comes just months after a controversial low Pensacola Beach flyover in July that sent debris flying, raising concern for public safety.

Maj. Scott Laux, a second-year member of the elite team, was identified as Blue Angel No. 6. The Chief of Naval Air Training (CNATRA) confirmed his removal to the Pensacola News Journal, saying the decision was announced Friday before the season finale at home in Pensacola.

NAVY SAYS NO REPRIMANDS OR FIRINGS AFTER BLUE ANGELS’ LOW PASS OVER BEACHGOERS

Blue Angels #6 opposing solo Maj. Scott Laux, USMC, answers media questions at NAS Pensacola on July 16, 2026 after the controversial low beach flyover.

"Blue Angel #6 was removed from the team for failing to uphold the standards expected of members of the Navy Flight Demonstration Squadron and will not participate in the team’s remaining performance this season," CNATRA’s public affairs office wrote in a statement Friday.

Fox News Digital reached out for further information Sunday morning and has not yet heard back.

Laux previously defended the team’s low-flying displays after the July flyover over Pensacola Beach sent tents, beach chairs and umbrellas flying as sand swept across the shoreline.

"We appreciate the trust in support and it’s our privilege to be able to perform in that way," Laux told Rolling with Madrina after the incident. "We’re gonna keep bringing the heat and continue doing it safely."

VIRAL VIDEO OF JETS BUZZING DHL STADIUM IN CAPE TOWN PROMPTS AVIATION SAFETY INVESTIGATION

Maj. Scott Laux spent one year as a narrator and most of his second year on the Blue Angels as opposing solo #6, before being shelved before the final performance of the season this weekend. (Getty Images)

Navy and War Department leaders had previously defended the low flyovers.

"Flight debrief complete. No reprimands. No firings. No problem," Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao wrote on X in July. "That’s the sound of Freedom! Semper fi and Hooyah."

War Secretary Pete Hegseth had vowed more support.

"The flyovers will continue until morale improves," Hegseth wrote on X.

The White House posted a photo meme of the controversial flyover from its official X account.

"It's okay to love America," the post read.

HEGSETH STEPS IN TO ‘FIX’ SITUATION AFTER APACHE PILOTS SUSPENDED FOR ‘SALUTE FROM THE SHORES’ FLYOVER

Marine Corps Maj. Scott Laux was outspoken in defending the July low beach flyover, but he is the one who has conspicuously been removed from the Blue Angels' final performance of the season. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

The Navy has not said when Laux was dismissed or what conduct prompted the decision. His photo and biography are no longer featured on the Blue Angels’ website's team page

Laux was absent from the squadron’s NAS Pensacola Homecoming Air Show on Friday and Saturday, where the team performed with five jets instead of its usual six. Laux's role was the opposing solo, which flies with lead solo #5 in the head-on crossing passes and mirror-image maneuvers that fill the gaps between the four-jet Diamond’s routines.

The routines were adjusted to account for the missing jet, according to reports.

The 2026 narrator, Lt. Commander Ronny Hafeza, might replace Laux on the 2027 team. The Blue Angels officers serve three-year terms, one as a narrator as Laux did.

Laux, a native of Chantilly, Va., graduated from the U.S. Naval Academy in 2012 with a degree in Chinese and earned his wings in 2015, according to his bio, which as of Sunday morning could still be accessed on the site despite no longer being listed with the rest of the team. He flew F/A-18 Hornets with Marine Corps squadrons, deployed to Japan and aboard the USS Nimitz and supported three operations during the 2020 carrier deployment: Resolute Support, Inherent Resolve and Octave Quartz.

A Blue Angels jet conducts a low pass over Pensacola Beach on Wednesday. (Partridge Drones via Facebook)

The Navy’s Blue Angels fly in formation over Pensacola Beach. (Stephen Lashbrook)

People gathered at Pensacola Beach to photograph and video Blue Angels jets conducting a flyover on Wednesday. (Partridge Drones via Facebook)

The Blue Angels take to the skies during a flight over Florida’s Gulf Coast on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. (Stephen Lashbrook)

The U.S. Navy Blue Angels fly over Pensacola Beach on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. (Stephen Lashbrook)

The U.S. Navy Blue Angels fly over a pier along the Pensacola Beach coastline on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. (Stephen Lashbrook)

The Blue Angels soar above the Florida coastline during a Wednesday flight. (Stephen Lashbrook)

Video shared online showed beachgoers cheering as a Blue Angels jet made a low pass over Pensacola Beach on Wednesday. (Partridge Drones via Facebook)

Video shared online showed beachgoers cheering as two Blue Angels jets made a low pass over Pensacola Beach on Wednesday. (Partridge Drones via Facebook)

He later transitioned to the F-35C Lightning II and served as an instructor pilot before joining the Blue Angels in September 2024. Before becoming Blue Angels #6, he served as the show's narrator.

Laux has more than 1,300 flight hours and 169 aircraft carrier landings. His awards include two Navy and Marine Corps Commendation Medals and multiple unit awards.
